full_judgment:
Mahmudul Amin Choudhury J: This Rule was issued calling upon the Deputy Commissioner, Feni and opposite party No.1 to show cause why the order dated 2-3-1996 passed by the learned Additional Sessions Judge, Feni in Criminal Revision No.15 of 1994 should not be quashed and set aside. The learned Additional Sessions Judge by the said order allowed the revisional application and directed for holding further inquiry in respect of GR Case No.105 of 1992 of the Court of the Magistrate, 2nd Class, Feni. 

 2. The short fact leading to this Rule is that, opposite party No.1 as informant on 25-6-1992 lodged FIR with Feni Police Station alleging that on the same day while the informant and her mother went to their paddy field with labourers to cultivate the land accused-persons named in the FIR who were armed with iron-rod, lathi, bamboo stick, etc. attacked the informant and her mother and the present petitioner No.1 dealt a lathi blow on the right fore-arm of the informant, accused No.2 struck on the right wrist with an iron-rod and accused-petitioners 4 and 5 also assaulted the informant, all causing injuries. The mother of the informant came to her rescue but she was also dealt a lathi blow which caused an injury. She was also assaulted by other accused-persons and one of the accused snatched away gold ornaments from opposite party No.1. Accused-petitioner No.3 also outraged the modesty of the informant. Police on receipt of the FIR took up investigation of the case and ultimately submitted charge-sheet and the petitioners were then placed on trial before the learned Magistrate, Second Class, Feni where seven witnesses have been examined from the side of the prosecution. The learned Magistrate on consideration of the evidence on record by judgment dated 27-12-93 acquitted the accused-petitioners. 

 3. On being aggrieved by this order of acquittal the informant moved the learned Sessions Judge, Feni under section 439A of the Code of Criminal Procedure in Criminal Revision No.15 of 1994. The learned Additional Sessions Judge, Feni on hearing both the sides by his judgment dated 2-3-1996 allowed the Revisional Application and sent the case for fresh trial with certain observations. The accused-petitioners then moved this Court and obtained the present Rule. 

 4. Mr ANM Gaziul Hoque, the learned Counsel appearing on behalf of the accused-petitioners, submits that the order of acquittal is an appealable order under section 417(1)(b) of the Code of Criminal Procedure and when the same is an appealable order no revisional application is maintainable, The learned Sessions Judge committed illegality in accepting the criminal revisional application and the learned Additional Sessions Judge also committed wrong in allowing the same. It is submitted that in such a case the State could have directed the Public Prosecutor to present an appeal before the learned Sessions Judge against the order of acquittal passed by the Magistrate and as the same has not been done the entertainment of the revisional application is bad in law. It is also submitted that there is nothing on record to show that the State earlier refused to prefer any appeal. In case of refusal by the State to prefer appeal then an aggrieved party may file a revisional application. But nothing has been produced to show that the State refused to prefer appeal against the order of acquittal. 

 5. Mr Md Nazrul Islam Talukder, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the informant opposite party No.1 on the other hand, submits that when the State has not preferred any appeal the informant has every right to move the Court in revision and the informant moved the learned Sessions Judge under section 439A of the Code of Criminal Procedure against the order of acquittal and the same was rightly accepted and disposed of. It is submitted that where the State has not filed any appeal against the order of acquittal passed by a Magistrate in a police case the informant is competent under section 439A of the Code of Criminal Procedure to prefer a revision before the learned Sessions Judge who can look into the legality and propriety of the order of acquittal and in support of his submission he placed reliance in the case of Amjad Hossain and others vs. State and another, reported in 16 BLD 111. The learned Advocate also placed reliance in the case of Kashem Ali vs. State & ors, reported in 9 BLD (AD) 13 wherein it has been held that a revisional application cannot be taken to the Court of Sessions or to the High Court Division if the party who is entitled to prefer appeal failed to file any appeal against the order of acquittal, that is, a revision at the instance of a party who could have appealed cannot be allowed to proceed with the revision. It is submitted that the present case is a police case and the opposite party No.1 who is the informant has/had no right to prefer any appeal against the order of acquittal though she is vitally interested in the result of the case as an informant. So, she may move the court of Sessions in revision against the order of acquittal which has been done and there is no illegality in the same. 

 6. Admittedly, opposite party No.1 as informant lodged the FIR and the case ended in charge-sheet and the petitioners were placed on trial before a Magistrate of the Second Class who passed the order of acquittal. It is also an admitted fact that the State has not preferred any appeal against the order of acquittal. Sub-section(5) of section 439 of the Code of Criminal Procedure provides that where under this Code an appeal lies and no appeal is brought, no proceeding by way of revision shall be entertained at the instance of the party who could have appealed. Emphasis is given here on the words at the instance of the party who could have appealed. Here in such cases the State has the right to prefer an appeal. The informant has no such right and if the State fail to prefer  appeal they cannot be allowed to prefer any revisional application. The embargo is only in respect of the person who could have appealed, that is, the State in the present case, Admittedly, the State has not preferred the revisional application. The same has been filed by the informant who is very much interested in the result of the original criminal case and present opposite party No.1 filed revisional application before the learned Sessions Judge which was heard and disposed of by the learned Additional Sessions Judge as aforesaid. The High Court Division following the principles of law enunciated in the case of Kasem Ali VS. State & ors, reported in 1989 BLD (AD) 13 found that where the State has not filed any appeal against the order of acquittal passed by a Magistrate in a police case the informant is competent under section 439A of the Code of Criminal Procedure to prefer revision before the learned Sessions Judge who can look into the legality or propriety of the order of acquittal. From the side of the petitioners no other contrary decision of any Division of this court has been brought to our notice. In section 439A of the CrPC it has been provided that the Sessions Judge may exercise, all or any of the powers which may be exercised by the High Court Division under section 439 of the CrPC. 

 7. Mr ANM Gaziul Haque submitted that the informant opposite party No.1 has not issued any notice upon the State to know whether they would prefer any appeal in the matter and when no such notice was issued the informant on her own cannot prefer any revisional application. But in support of his submission Mr Hoque failed to place any decision of this court or any law or rules that may be framed. He submitted that it is the practice that such notices are issued. It is true that in cases of acquittal notices are issued by the informant to the State to know whether they would prefer any appeal and on receipt of the reply in the negative revisional applications are filed. The reason behind this is that if and when an appeal is filed the revisional application would become redundant and further reason is that it is the practice of the court to file revisional applications within 60 days from the date of the order and notices are issued it appears to save such limitations. But in case where no notice is issued and an appeal and a revision is filed then revisional application will have its natural death in view of the filing of the appeal. But mere non-issuance of any notice cannot by itself be a bar in filing the revisional application against the order of acquittal. In view of this we find no force in the argument advanced by Mr. Hoque in this respect. 

 8. It may be pointed out there that if no appeal is preferred from the side of the State in a police case the informant cannot be gagged in moving the Court in revision as "with the change of time and circumstances attending the administration of criminal justice time has come and experience also demand that High Court Division will have to be a little more scrutinizing even In a case of acquittal because in the ultimate analysis it is the interest of public justice and or prevention of miscarriage of justice which prompt the Court of revision to interfere in a particular case." "The Court of revision can legitimately examine whether correct principles relating to appraisal of evidence has been followed or not, whether some material piece of evidence has been overlooked or misappreciated which could have a profound bearing on the order of acquittal and things like that". That is the view of our Appellate Division in the case reported in 9 BLD (AD) 13 (Kashem Ali VS. State & Ors). 

 9. Thus, after consideration of the points of law involved, we hold that Mr ANM Gaziul Hoque failed to make out any case for our interference in this revisional application.
